prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states there, which opened the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B013 as my single preferred part, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. Nothing said in round 1 moved the core of the case, and several things sharpened it. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model made a sharp, falsifiable prediction (flat bands at a specific twist angle), and nature answered with a result nobody had asked for: a tunable carbon system that gives correlated insulators and superconductivity from one knob. That is a clue from nature of exactly the kind I care about, not elegant theory left unconfirmed. Independent groups in graphene multilayers and TMD moire systems have since reproduced the phenomena, and spectroscopy and scanning probes agree with the flat-band picture, so what a prize would cite does not depend on the pairing mechanism, any more than the 1987 cuprate prize waited for a theory of high-Tc. The theory-plus-experiment trio sits inside the supplied names, which makes it the cleanest allocation among the candidates that are genuinely new physics. I am keeping the citation to the discovery and the platform, and I would not word it as a statement about the origin of the superconductivity.
statement.case_against: I do not dismiss the maturity objection, which I share more than my vote suggests. Under a decade of work, large sample-to-sample variation and an unsettled pairing mechanism mean the long-term weight of the field is not yet demonstrated, and I have said in print that big ideas can take a long time to show their worth. The attribution gap is real: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, and the earlier band-structure work (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Suarez Morell and colleagues) are outside the credited names, and the three-name limit forbids a fix. None of us has checked this from the record, only from memory, and as Secretary I would insist that the expert reports answer it before any decision rather than after. If that answer is that decisive experimental credit is genuinely diffuse, or that earlier theory anticipated the magic-angle result in substance, I would withdraw from B013 and move to B061.

responses.point: Kroll holds B061 first as the most reproducible and cleanly attributed result, calls it an engineering-physics achievement rather than a new phenomenon, and says he cannot judge the condensed-matter details of B013 himself.
responses.response: Your candour about it being engineering physics is exactly why I still lean the other way: the committee has said before that the discoveries are at the centre, and a new regime of correlated matter in a tunable platform is closer to a discovery than a better clock. But your answer on attribution is the stronger one and I do not wave it away: Katori and Ye are a pair where seven of eight of us named identical names, and that is worth more than I gave it in round 1. To the chair's question, I could accept B061 with your narrow wording (the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and its control to 10^-18) and the condition is the one I state above: if the record on B013 shows the credit is not defensible, or if the committee concludes maturity must come first, I move to B061 without regret.

responses.point: Eriksson raises that a second condensed-matter prize soon after the 2016 topological-phases prize could shift the committee toward AMO or precision measurement, and that sample dependence is large in the graphene devices.
responses.response: I would not let the 2016 prize count much. Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phases and transitions in the abstract; moire flat-band physics is a different phenomenon and a different experimental platform, and the committee does not ration by subfield when the discovery is distinct. I take the sample-dependence point more seriously, but it has the same answer as for early cuprates: the reproducibility across many groups is in the qualitative phases, not in the exact critical temperatures, and the prize would cite the qualitative result. Where I agree with you is that your own B019 alternative has the better allocation problem than you allow, since the HgTe prediction and the 3D work sit outside the trio, and so I would still not move to it.

responses.point: Mehlig says that if the pairing mechanism must be understood first, B013 is early and B061 or B008 are safer, and asks whether members who ranked B061 first would prefer it on maturity grounds.
responses.response: I am on the opposite side of your conditional but I accept the logic of it. My answer to the chair's second question is that an unresolved pairing mechanism is not by itself a reason to wait, because the discovery is the platform and the correlated phases, and the evidence that would settle it is simple: independent reproduction of insulating and superconducting states beyond the original lab, which we already have. What would change my mind is not the mechanism but a failure of the priority record. I do not share your inclination to B008: Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase are two quite different discoveries bridged by a theme, as you said yourself, and the three-name limit makes that bridge impossible to honour fairly.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B061 first on instrument and reproducibility grounds, holds no strong view between B061 and B013, and says he would support IceCube in a later year but cannot chair a consensus around it now.
responses.response: I accept your assessment of B009 and I have kept it as the second alternative only as a marker for a later year: the diffuse flux is secure, but the source identifications lack a second detector and the AMANDA and Baikal founders make a two-name citation harder than I implied in round 1. On the chair's question about a fixed attribution as a condition, I think the committee should be honest that we are choosing between a discovery with a messy credit chain and a measurement with a clean one, and that a 4-4 split is information about that trade-off, not a reason to split the difference. I would rather lose the argument than rank by headcount.

responses.point: Olsson supports B013 under the mandate of an experimentally verified discovery with an original experiment, but wants to be certain the credited people did the original work before settling, and challenged whether I can name the first detection for IceCube.
responses.response: On the first point we are aligned and I take your caution as the right one: I would like the Secretary's expert reports to settle whether the decisive 2018 experiment belongs to Jarillo-Herrero's group as a whole and whether Cao's role is that of a student on a group-leader experiment, which is the normal prize convention but should be checked, not assumed. On IceCube your objection about the first detection versus leading the programme is fair, and I concede it: it is the reason I moved it to an alternative, and the founding credit is spread across DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA. I would hold you to the same test on B013, and I think it passes, because the experiment that found the correlated states is one we can name.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record on the Bistritzer-MacDonald model, the earlier band-structure work and the 2018 experiments supports crediting MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer as the decisive trio, or whether Yuan Cao and earlier theory carry enough priority to make this unacceptable. My knowledge is from memory.
Whether the committee regards a field under a decade old, with an unsettled pairing mechanism, as mature enough this year.
Whether the 4-4 split between B013 and B061 reflects a real difference in judgement on discovery versus measurement or only on timing.
Whether the IceCube source identifications will gain independent confirmation, which would change the standing of B009 in a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B013, B061 or B009. I have Princeton and Uppsala ties and co-authors in string theory and cosmology, none connected to the credited people, and no collaboration with any shortlisted candidate. As Secretary I am responsible for the expert reports, which is a procedural role and not a conflict.
